entities.summary:
Charles de Lorraine de Vaudémont, born on April 30, 1561, in Nomeny, was a French Roman Catholic cardinal and bishop whose brief but politically charged life unfolded amidst the turbulent French Wars of Religion. As the third son of Nicolas de Lorraine, Duke of Mercœur, and a member of the powerful House of Guise through his maternal lineage, his ecclesiastical career was deeply intertwined with the dynastic ambitions and Catholic militancy of his family. Elevated to the bishopric of Verdun at the precocious age of ten in 1572 and subsequently created a cardinal by Pope Gregory XIII in 1578, he epitomized the aristocratic practice of securing high church offices for younger sons to consolidate familial power and influence within the Gallican Church and the wider European Catholic hierarchy.

His early ascent within the Church positioned him as a significant, albeit young, figure for the ultra-Catholic faction in France. Though he never received major episcopal consecration or actively governed his diocese due to his youth and the political climate, his cardinalate provided the House of Guise with another voice in Rome and a potential leader for the Counter-Reformation movement in France. He participated in diplomatic missions on behalf of his family, including efforts to secure Spanish support for the Catholic League, a fiercely anti-Huguenot and anti-royalist faction. His close kinship to figures like Henri, Duke of Guise, placed him at the heart of the factional struggles that defined late 16th-century France.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Charles de Lorraine de Vaudémont's role as a cardinal and bishop from the powerful House of Guise highlights the intersection of aristocratic power and religious office during the French Wars of Religion, influencing the political landscape of the Catholic League. His career, though brief, exemplifies the strategic use of ecclesiastical positions to consolidate dynastic and ideological influence within France.
